guide.sub: Four decades of back-road stories, gathered into one trip through Mule Town — the courthouse square, the banks of the Duck River, and the makers, mealhouses, and mule-day traditions our hosts found along the way.
guide.metaNote: every one a real Crossroads segment
guide.mapLede: Every stop our cameras visited, plotted from the square to the county line.
guide.quote: “Come travel the highways and by-ways of Tennessee.”
guide.note: We hope this guide leads you to new memories, a hidden gem, or someplace you’ve always meant to visit. Thanks for making Tennessee Crossroads part of your journey.
guide.colophonHTML: Tennessee Crossroads is a Nashville PBS production · Each place began as a story on the show

print.coverCaption: The James K. Polk Home, West 7th Street

sections.title: Eat & Drink
sections.intro: Catfish trays off the beaten path, pies on the square, and a taste of New Orleans on the Duck River.

stops.name: Catfish Campus Restaurant
stops.blurb: A catfish restaurant off the beaten path that packs them in six days a week. Tammi Arender heads to class at Columbia's Catfish Campus.

stops.name: The Dotted Lime
stops.blurb: Miranda Cohen found a friendly little place in Columbia serving delicious food — and peace of mind — for everyone at the table.

stops.name: Marcy Jo's Mealhouse and Bakery
stops.blurb: Ken Wilshire visits an old mercantile store that's brought new life back to Pottsville — now a mealhouse and bakery worth the drive down Highway 431.

stops.name: Pie Sensations
stops.blurb: Tennessee Crossroads found a tiny place turning out pies with mighty big flavor. Rob Wilds saves room for dessert at Pie Sensations, right on Columbia's square.

stops.name: River Terrace Restaurant
stops.blurb: A pair of New Orleans transplants resettled in Columbia after Hurricane Katrina, restored an old restaurant on the Duck River, and brought the taste of home with them. Joe Elmore pulls up to the riverbank.

sections.title: See & Explore
sections.intro: A president's home place, a festival ruled by mules, and trains you can ride in miniature.

stops.name: James K. Polk Home
stops.blurb: Three presidents claimed Tennessee home, but only one went to Washington, did what he said he'd do, and came home without fanfare. Rob Wilds tours the Columbia home of James K. Polk.

stops.name: Mule Day
stops.blurb: Once a year, the mighty mule rules the day in Columbia — parade, pageantry, and all the reasons they call this Mule Town. Sharon Puckett joins the celebration, held late March to early April. Seasonal.

stops.name: Mid-South Live Steamers
stops.blurb: At Maury County Park, the Mid-South Live Steamers share the joy of riding the rails in a small way — miniature locomotives with full-size devotion. Check the club's schedule for public ride days.

sections.title: Makers
sections.intro: Signs that glow, negatives saved from the attic of history, and old trucks made showroom-new.

stops.name: Columbia Neon
stops.blurb: The folks at Columbia Neon have been lighting candles — electric ones — since the Great Depression. Susan Watson stops by the Nashville Highway shop where the craft still glows.

stops.name: West Seventh Company
stops.blurb: When Columbians uncovered more than a million photographic negatives — some dating back to 1870 — they knew they'd found buried treasure. Rob Wilds sees pictures of the past preserved at West Seventh Company.

stops.name: Possum Holler Garage
stops.blurb: On the backroads of Maury County, Max Davis never met an old truck he didn't like — and he can transform one into a show-quality masterpiece. Joe Elmore finds Possum Holler Garage, off the beaten path.

sections.title: Crossroads Characters
sections.intro: Whittlers, collectors, and the friendly faces our hosts met along the way.

stops.name: Wood Den Carvers
stops.blurb: Cutting pieces of wood and trading cutting remarks — the Wood Den Carvers prove a hobby is better with friends. Rob Wilds joins Columbia's merry band of whittlers.

stops.name: Kathie & Steve Fuston, Clock Collectors
stops.blurb: In a digital age, Kathie and Steve Fuston still appreciate clocks as the intricate, beautiful devices they are. Rob Wilds visits the Columbia collectors and their wonderful gallery of timekeepers.

stops.name: Billy Roy Parks, Wood Carver
stops.blurb: Whittling has always passed the time down on the farm, and this Columbia farmer carved out quite a niche — a collection of artwork more than seven decades in the making.

sections.title: Stay a While
sections.intro: One gracious place to rest up before tomorrow's back roads.

stops.name: Blythewood Inn Bed & Breakfast
stops.blurb: The Blythewood Inn offers guests a trip back to a quieter, more gracious time. Rob Wilds checks in at the Columbia bed and breakfast.
